reaction.periodic_elements.lawrencium_sy: Californium bombarded with boron (Ghiorso 1961): a few atoms of lawrencium, known only by the decay chain the detectors record; put boron in the reagent slot
reaction.periodic_elements.rutherfordium: Californium bombarded with carbon (Ghiorso 1969): a few atoms of rutherfordium, known only by the decay chain the detectors record; put carbon in the reagent slot
reaction.periodic_elements.dubnium_synth: Californium bombarded with nitrogen (Ghiorso 1970): a few atoms of dubnium, known only by the decay chain the detectors record; put nitrogen in the reagent slot
reaction.periodic_elements.seaborgium_sy: Californium bombarded with oxygen (Ghiorso 1974): a few atoms of seaborgium, known only by the decay chain the detectors record; put oxygen in the reagent slot
reaction.periodic_elements.bohrium_synth: Bismuth bombarded with chromium (Munzenberg, GSI 1981): a few atoms of bohrium, known only by the decay chain the detectors record; put chromium in the reagent slot
reaction.periodic_elements.hassium_synth: Lead bombarded with iron (GSI 1984): a few atoms of hassium, known only by the decay chain the detectors record; put iron in the reagent slot
reaction.periodic_elements.meitnerium_sy: Bismuth bombarded with iron (GSI 1982): a few atoms of meitnerium, known only by the decay chain the detectors record; put iron in the reagent slot
reaction.periodic_elements.darmstadtium_: Lead bombarded with nickel (Hofmann, GSI 1994): a few atoms of darmstadtium, known only by the decay chain the detectors record; put nickel in the reagent slot
reaction.periodic_elements.roentgenium_s: Bismuth bombarded with nickel (GSI 1994): a few atoms of roentgenium, known only by the decay chain the detectors record; put nickel in the reagent slot
reaction.periodic_elements.copernicium_s: Lead bombarded with zinc (GSI 1996): a few atoms of copernicium, known only by the decay chain the detectors record; put zinc in the reagent slot
reaction.periodic_elements.nihonium_synt: Bismuth bombarded with zinc (Morita, RIKEN 2004): a few atoms of nihonium, known only by the decay chain the detectors record; put zinc in the reagent slot
reaction.periodic_elements.flerovium_syn: Plutonium bombarded with calcium-48 (Oganessian, Dubna 1999): a few atoms of flerovium, known only by the decay chain the detectors record; put calcium-48 in the reagent slot
reaction.periodic_elements.moscovium_syn: Americium bombarded with calcium-48 (Dubna 2004): a few atoms of moscovium, known only by the decay chain the detectors record; put calcium-48 in the reagent slot
reaction.periodic_elements.livermorium_s: Curium bombarded with calcium-48 (Dubna 2000): a few atoms of livermorium, known only by the decay chain the detectors record; put calcium-48 in the reagent slot
reaction.periodic_elements.tennessine_sy: Berkelium from Oak Ridge bombarded with calcium-48 (Dubna 2010): a few atoms of tennessine, known only by the decay chain the detectors record; put calcium-48 in the reagent slot
reaction.periodic_elements.oganesson_syn: Californium bombarded with calcium-48 (Dubna 2002): a few atoms of oganesson, known only by the decay chain the detectors record; put calcium-48 in the reagent slot
reaction.periodic_elements.lithium_cobal: Cobalt fired in air with lithium: layered LiCoO2 that lets lithium ions in and out (Goodenough and Mizushima 1980); put lithium in the reagent slot
reaction.periodic_elements.optical_fibre: Pure silica doped with a trace of erbium, melted and drawn into fibre: a pumped erbium fibre amplifies light without turning it into current (Payne and Desurvire 1987); put erbium in the reagent slot
reaction.periodic_elements.shale_retorti: Oil shale heated in a closed retort: kerogen cracks into shale oil and gas, and char stays in the spent rock (Young's paraffin works 1851)
reaction.periodic_elements.crude_distill: Crude oil boiled up a column: gas at the top (burnt under the still), then naphtha, kerosene and diesel; bitumen stays in the still and comes out as its residue (Drake's well 1859)
reaction.periodic_elements.diesel_cracki: Heavy oil held hot under pressure breaks into gasoline, ethylene and gas, leaving coke (Burton 1913)
reaction.periodic_elements.naphtha_refor: Naphtha over a platinum catalyst: chains close into rings and give up hydrogen, which the refinery uses itself (UOP Platforming 1949)
reaction.periodic_elements.coal_hydrogen: Powdered coal and hydrogen at 200 atm become petrol and middle oil (Bergius 1913); put hydrogen in the reagent slot
reaction.periodic_elements.coal_deoxygen: The oxygen in coal leaves as water; put hydrogen in the reagent slot
reaction.periodic_elements.coal_desulfur: The sulfur in coal leaves as hydrogen sulfide; put hydrogen in the reagent slot
reaction.periodic_elements.pvc_synthesis: Ethylene and chlorine give dichloroethane, which cracks to vinyl chloride and hydrogen chloride; the vinyl chloride polymerises to PVC (Semon 1926); put chlorine in the reagent slot
reaction.periodic_elements.polyethylene_: Ethylene at 1500 atm with a trace of oxygen turns to a white waxy solid (Fawcett and Gibson at ICI 1933); with chlorine in the reagent slot you get PVC instead
reaction.periodic_elements.nylon_synthes: Game shortcut for Carothers' nylon 6-6 (DuPont 1935): benzene becomes adipic acid and hexamethylenediamine, whose nitrogen comes from ammonia, and the two join into fibre; put ammonia in the reagent slot
reaction.periodic_elements.xylene_oxidat: p-Xylene oxidised by air in acetic acid over cobalt and manganese (Amoco 1958): terephthalic acid crystallises out
reaction.periodic_elements.benzene_nitra: Benzene stirred with nitric and sulfuric acids gives yellow, almond-smelling nitrobenzene (Mitscherlich 1834); put nitric acid in the reagent slot
reaction.periodic_elements.ppd_synthesis: Game shortcut for the nitroaniline route: nitrobenzene and ammonia end up as p-phenylenediamine; put ammonia in the reagent slot
reaction.periodic_elements.aramid_polyme: Kwolek's aramid (DuPont 1965): the acid's chloride and p-phenylenediamine join in long stiff chains, spun from sulfuric acid into Kevlar; put p-phenylenediamine in the reagent slot
reaction.periodic_elements.uranium_235_s: Uranium ions bent round the magnet in Lawrence's Y-12 calutrons (1944): a twentieth of the metal comes out with twenty times the odds of U-235, and the rest is depleted
reaction.periodic_elements.lithium_6_sep: Lithium-6 lands in its own pocket: 7% of the lithium comes out as nearly pure lithium-6, the rest is lithium-7
reaction.periodic_elements.boron_10_sepa: Boron-10, the strong neutron absorber, parted from boron-11: a fifth of the boron comes out over 90% boron-10
reaction.periodic_elements.enriched_meta: Uranium metal with at least 3% U-235 burnt to oxide and sintered into fuel pellets; richer metal makes the same pellets
reaction.periodic_elements.heavy_water_e: Girdler sulfide towers trade deuterium between water and hydrogen sulfide, hot and cold, until the water is almost pure D2O (1943); game-boosted 50 times
reaction.periodic_elements.control_rod_p: Boron with at least 90% boron-10 sintered into a steel-clad rod: one in a reactor's slots holds the chain reaction back while the reactor is full
reaction.periodic_elements.biodiesel_tal: Fat stirred warm with methanol and a little lye: methyl esters for diesel engines, glycerol below (Chavanne 1937); put methanol in the reagent slot
reaction.periodic_elements.biodiesel_oil: Plant oil stirred warm with methanol and a little lye: biodiesel and glycerol (Chavanne 1937); put methanol in the reagent slot
Fat boiled with lye from wood ash: soft potash soap, with glycerol in the liquor; put wood ash in the reagent slot
reaction.periodic_elements.oil_soap_boil: Oil boiled with lye from wood ash makes soft soap too; put wood ash in the reagent slot
reaction.periodic_elements.hard_soap_boi: Fat boiled with soda ash: hard soap that sets in bars (Marseille, Castile); put sodium carbonate in the reagent slot
Common salt thrown into soft soap turns it to hard soda soap; put salt in the reagent slot
reaction.periodic_elements.rendering.des: Meat, bone and fat simmered: the tallow floats off and greaves and bone are left as protein meal
reaction.periodic_elements.greaves.desc: The meat and gristle left when the fat is rendered: greaves, pressed into protein meal
reaction.periodic_elements.bone_meal_ren: Boiled bone is ground into the meal with the greaves
Seeds crushed in a screw press: oil runs out and the cake is left; put empty flasks in the flask slot
reaction.periodic_elements.pit_tanning.d: Hides laid in bark liquor for months: tannin binds the protein into leather; put oak or spruce logs in the reagent slot
reaction.periodic_elements.abe_fermentat: Weizmann's bacterium ferments starch to acetone, butanol and ethanol, 3:6:1 (1916); put calcite in the reagent slot to keep the mash from souring
reaction.periodic_elements.starch_mashin: Malted grain turns the starch of a mash into sugar
reaction.periodic_elements.glucose_ferme: C6H12O6 -> 2 C2H5OH + 2 CO2: the sugar of a mash ferments to alcohol
reaction.periodic_elements.ether_distill: Spirit distilled with oil of vitriol gives sweet oil of vitriol, ether (Frobenius 1730); put sulfuric acid in the reagent slot
reaction.periodic_elements.clay_sulfatio: Clay boiled in oil of vitriol: the alumina dissolves as sulfate and the silica stays; put sulfuric acid in the reagent slot
reaction.periodic_elements.alum_crystall: Potash added to the sulfate liquor and it cools: alum crystallizes in octahedra; put wood ash in the reagent slot
reaction.periodic_elements.ammonium_sulf: Ammonia water neutralised with sulfuric acid and boiled down: sulfate of ammonia for the fields; put sulfuric acid in the reagent slot
reaction.periodic_elements.superphosphat: Bones or phosphate rock in sulfuric acid: phosphate plants can take up (Lawes 1842); put sulfuric acid in the reagent slot
reaction.periodic_elements.starch_hydrol: Starch boiled with a little acid becomes sugar; chalk takes the acid out after (Kirchhoff 1811); put sulfuric acid in the reagent slot
reaction.periodic_elements.vulcanization: Rubber heated with sulfur under steam pressure cures tough and springy (Goodyear 1839); put sulfur in the reagent slot
Latex dried in the steam pan: the water goes, raw rubber is left
reaction.periodic_elements.tar_distillat: Coal tar cut by boiling point: light oil (benzene and toluene), carbolic oil (phenol), anthracene oil; pitch stays in the still (Mansfield 1848)
reaction.periodic_elements.prussiate_mak: Dried blood calcined with potash gives yellow prussiate; green vitriol throws down Prussian blue (Diesbach 1706); put green vitriol in the reagent slot
reaction.periodic_elements.blue_dyeing.d: Prussian blue ground and washed into blue dye: 8 dyes to an item of pigment
reaction.periodic_elements.fuchsine_maki: Aniline heated with arsenic acid turns magenta (Verguin 1858); put white arsenic in the reagent slot
reaction.periodic_elements.magenta_dyein: Fuchsine dissolved and struck onto a base: 32 magenta dyes to a flask's worth
reaction.periodic_elements.red_dyeing.de: Alizarin laked into Turkey red: 32 red dyes to a flask's worth
reaction.periodic_elements.yellow_dyeing: Picric acid dyes silk a clear yellow: 32 yellow dyes to a flask's worth
reaction.periodic_elements.aniline_reduc: Nitrobenzene stirred with iron filings and a little acid becomes aniline (Bechamp 1854); put iron in the reagent slot
reaction.periodic_elements.picric_acid_m: Phenol nitrated three times: yellow picric acid (Woulfe 1771); put nitric acid in the reagent slot
reaction.periodic_elements.nitroglycerin: Glycerol dripped into cold mixed acid, kept under 25 °C (Sobrero 1847); put nitric acid in the reagent slot
reaction.periodic_elements.cordite_makin: Nitroglycerin and guncotton kneaded with acetone and pressed into cords (Abel and Dewar 1889); put smokeless powder in the reagent slot
reaction.periodic_elements.aspirin_makin: Salicylic acid acetylated (Hoffmann 1897; acetic acid stands in for the anhydride); put acetic acid in the reagent slot
reaction.periodic_elements.alizarin_fusi: Game shortcut for oxidation, sulfonation and fusion with caustic soda under pressure: anthracene to alizarin (Graebe, Liebermann, Caro 1869); put sodium hydroxide in the reagent slot
reaction.periodic_elements.kolbe_schmitt: Phenol with soda and carbon dioxide at 5 atm and 125 °C gives salicylic acid (Kolbe 1860, Schmitt 1885); put sodium carbonate in the reagent slot
reaction.periodic_elements.pyrethrum_gri: Dried oxeye daisy heads ground fine: Dalmatian insect powder
reaction.periodic_elements.copper_vitrio: Copper dissolved in hot oil of vitriol crystallizes as blue vitriol; put sulfuric acid in the reagent slot
reaction.periodic_elements.carbide_smelt: CaO + 3 C -> CaC2 + CO: quicklime fused with coke in the arc (Willson 1892); put coke in the fuel slot
reaction.periodic_elements.acetylene_gen: CaC2 + 2 H2O -> C2H2 + Ca(OH)2: water dripped on carbide gives acetylene, slaked lime stays; put water in the reagent slot
reaction.periodic_elements.cyanamide_mak: CaC2 + N2 -> CaCN2 + C: carbide heated in nitrogen takes it up as nitrolime (Frank and Caro 1898); put nitrogen in the reagent slot
reaction.periodic_elements.formaldehyde_: CH3OH + 1/2 O2 -> HCHO + H2O: wood spirit and air over red-hot silver gauze (Hofmann 1867)
reaction.periodic_elements.bakelite_maki: Phenol and formaldehyde cooked under pressure set hard into Bakelite (Baekeland 1907); put formaldehyde in the reagent slot
reaction.periodic_elements.urea_synthesi: 2 NH3 + CO2 -> CO(NH2)2 + H2O at 150 atm and 180 °C (Bosch and Meiser 1922); put carbon dioxide (caught with a Gas Recovery Hood) in the reagent slot
reaction.periodic_elements.an_neutralizi: NH3 + HNO3 -> NH4NO3: ammonia and nitric acid neutralise each other, and the hot melt falls down the tower as prills; put nitric acid in the reagent slot
Molten urea with superphosphate and potash, sprayed from the top of the tower: NPK prills; put PK Blend in the reagent slot
reaction.periodic_elements.tnt_making.de: Toluene nitrated three times over: trinitrotoluene, TNT (Wilbrand 1863); put nitric acid in the reagent slot
reaction.periodic_elements.neoprene_maki: Game shortcut for DuPont's route: acetylene doubled over copper chloride, joined with hydrogen chloride into chloroprene and polymerized (Carothers 1931); put hydrochloric acid in the reagent slot
reaction.periodic_elements.lebedev_butad: 2 C2H5OH -> C4H6 + 2 H2O + H2: alcohol vapour over zinc oxide and alumina (Lebedev 1926)
reaction.periodic_elements.styrene_makin: Game shortcut: benzene joined with ethylene, then the ethylbenzene stripped of hydrogen into styrene (IG Farben 1930); put ethylene in the reagent slot
reaction.periodic_elements.buna_polymeri: Butadiene and styrene stirred in soapy water until they join: Buna-S rubber (IG Farben 1929); put styrene in the reagent slot
reaction.periodic_elements.sulfanilamide: Game shortcut for the chlorosulfonic acid route: aniline sulfonated and aminated into sulfanilamide (Domagk 1932, Trefouel 1935); put ammonium sulfate in the reagent slot
reaction.periodic_elements.polystyrene_m: Styrene heated until its molecules join into polystyrene (BASF 1930); blown with gas, it is foam (Dow 1941)
reaction.periodic_elements.penicillin_fe: Mould from a Peoria melon grown in stirred, aerated tanks of sugar and corn steep: penicillin (Florey, Chain, Moyer 1943); put milk in the reagent slot for its lactose
reaction.periodic_elements.streptomycin_: A soil bacterium fed sugar and protein makes streptomycin (Schatz and Waksman 1943); put protein meal in the reagent slot
reaction.periodic_elements.ddt_making.de: Game shortcut for chloral and chlorobenzene in oil of vitriol: benzene and chlorine end as DDT (Zeidler 1874, Muller 1939); put chlorine in the reagent slot
reaction.periodic_elements.two_four_d_ma: Game shortcut: phenol chlorinated and joined to chloroacetic acid, 2,4-D (Pokorny 1941; sold 1945); put chlorine in the reagent slot
reaction.periodic_elements.atrazine_maki: Game shortcut for cyanuric chloride and amines: ammonia, chlorine and carbon end as atrazine (Geigy 1958); put chlorine in the reagent slot and coke in the fuel slot
reaction.periodic_elements.hexamine_maki: 6 HCHO + 4 NH3 -> (CH2)6N4 + 6 H2O: formaldehyde and ammonia crystallize as hexamine (Butlerov 1859); put ammonia in the reagent slot
reaction.periodic_elements.rdx_making.de: Hexamine nitrated cold in strong nitric acid gives RDX (Henning 1898, Woolwich 1940s); put nitric acid in the reagent slot
reaction.periodic_elements.iodide_making: Sodium iodide from kelp ash and potash salt trade places: potassium iodide crystallizes; put potassium chloride in the reagent slot
reaction.periodic_elements.glyphosate_ma: Game shortcut for glycine, formaldehyde and phosphorous acid: glyphosate (Franz, Monsanto 1970); put phosphoric acid in the reagent slot
reaction.periodic_elements.cellulose_fer: Enzymes from engineered fungi break cellulose to sugar, and yeast ferments it to ethanol: fuel from any plant (2000s)
reaction.periodic_elements.pla_making.de: Bacteria ferment sugar to lactic acid, which is joined into polylactic acid, PLA (NatureWorks 2001)
reaction.periodic_elements.vaccine_makin: Game shortcut: messenger RNA copied from a DNA template and wrapped in fat droplets (Kariko and Weissman 2005; 2020); put vegetable oil in the reagent slot
reaction.periodic_elements.amifostine_ma: Game shortcut for the Walter Reed thiophosphate: phosphoric acid with ammonia and sulfur ends as amifostine (1959; approved 1995); put ammonium sulfate in the reagent slot
reaction.periodic_elements.air_compressi: Air squeezed to eight atmospheres for the rock drills (Sommeiller, Mont Cenis 1861)
reaction.periodic_elements.resin_distill: Pine resin distilled with steam: turpentine comes over, rosin stays in the pot
reaction.periodic_elements.quinine_extra: Cinchona bark steeped in dilute acid gives up its quinine (Pelletier and Caventou 1820)
Cinnamon bark distilled with steam: the oil of cinnamon comes over
reaction.periodic_elements.camphor_disti: Camphor wood distilled with steam: camphor crystallizes from the vapour
reaction.periodic_elements.eucalyptol_di: Eucalyptus leaves distilled with steam: the oil comes over
reaction.periodic_elements.santalol_dist: Sandalwood distilled with steam: sandalwood oil comes over
reaction.periodic_elements.brazilin_dyei: Brazilwood chips boiled and laked with alum: 32 red dyes to a flask's worth
reaction.periodic_elements.sugar_crystal: Maple or palm sap boiled down: the sugar stays when the water has gone
reaction.periodic_elements.salicin_extra: Willow bark steeped in hot water gives up its salicin (Leroux 1829)
reaction.periodic_elements.salicin_oxida: Salicin split and oxidised: salicylic acid from willow bark (Piria 1838); put oxygen in the reagent slot
reaction.periodic_elements.cedrol_distil: Cedar wood distilled with steam: cedarwood oil comes over
reaction.periodic_elements.taxol_extract: Yew needles extracted with solvent and purified: a few milligrams of taxol from a whole tree (Wall and Wani 1971)
reaction.periodic_elements.citric_acid_c: Lemon juice limed and set free with sulfuric acid: citric acid crystallizes (Scheele 1784)
reaction.periodic_elements.jojoba_pressi: Jojoba seeds crushed in the screw press: a liquid wax runs out; put empty flasks in the flask slot
reaction.periodic_elements.wax_boiling.d: Waxy stems boiled in water soured with a little acid: the wax floats up and is skimmed off
Annatto seeds rubbed in warm alkaline water: the orange-red paste dyes like the Amazon body paint
reaction.periodic_elements.lawsone_dyein: Henna leaves ground and wetted: the red-brown paste stains wool and leather
reaction.periodic_elements.linalool_dist: Flowers distilled with steam: an oil of linalool comes over
reaction.periodic_elements.caffeine_extr: Tea leaves or guarana seeds steeped hot, the tannin limed out: caffeine crystallizes (Runge 1819)
reaction.periodic_elements.capsaicin_ext: Dried peppers soaked in alcohol: the burning capsaicin is left when it evaporates (Thresh 1876)
reaction.periodic_elements.emetine_extra: Ipecac root steeped in acid water and made alkaline: emetine comes down (Pelletier 1817)
reaction.periodic_elements.pilocarpine_e: Jaborandi leaves steeped in acid water and made alkaline: pilocarpine comes out (1875)
reaction.periodic_elements.ndga_extracti: Creosote leaves extracted with alcohol: NDGA crystallizes, an antioxidant for lard (1943)
reaction.periodic_elements.geraniol_dist: Rose petals distilled with steam: attar of roses comes over, rich in geraniol
reaction.periodic_elements.vitamin_c_ext: Rose hips, currants or cloudberries pressed and the juice concentrated cool: ascorbic acid crystallizes (Szent-Györgyi 1928)
reaction.periodic_elements.arbutin_extra: Bearberry leaves steeped in hot water, the tannin taken out with lead acetate: arbutin crystallizes
reaction.periodic_elements.indigo_dyeing: Indigo leaves steeped and fermented in the vat; the cloth turns blue in the air: 32 blue dyes to a flask's worth
reaction.periodic_elements.madder_dyeing: Madder root ground and boiled with alum: the old Turkey red: 32 red dyes to a flask's worth
reaction.periodic_elements.cobalt_60_act: Deuterons from heavy water fired at cobalt-59 make cobalt-60 (Co-59 + d -> Co-60 + p), a strong gamma source; put heavy water in the reagent slot
reaction.periodic_elements.carmine_dyein: Dried cochineal boiled with alum and a little tin: the scarlet of cardinals and redcoats
reaction.periodic_elements.shellac_refin: Sticklac washed in hot water and melted through a cloth: seedlac, then flakes of shellac
reaction.periodic_elements.hirudin_extra: Leech heads minced in cold salt water and the extract purified: hirudin, the first anticoagulant (Haycraft 1884)
reaction.periodic_elements.exenatide_mak: Exendin-4, found in Gila monster saliva, made by engineered bacteria: exenatide, a diabetes medicine (Eng 1992)
reaction.periodic_elements.guano_saltpet: Guano leached with hot water and potash lye, the liquor boiled down: saltpetre crystallizes
reaction.periodic_elements.galalith_maki: Casein curdled from skim milk, pressed and soaked in formalin for weeks: galalith; put formaldehyde in the reagent slot
reaction.periodic_elements.tyrian_purple: Murex glands crushed, left in the sun and boiled in lead vats: the purple of Tyre
reaction.periodic_elements.vitamin_d_ext: Liver oil boiled with lye and the part that will not become soap crystallized: vitamin D3 (Windaus 1936)
reaction.periodic_elements.chitosan_maki: Crab shells freed of lime in acid, then boiled in strong lye: chitin becomes chitosan
reaction.periodic_elements.lal_extractio: The blood cells of the horseshoe crab spun out cold and burst in pure water: Limulus amebocyte lysate
reaction.periodic_elements.gfp_making.de: The jellyfish gene for GFP put into bacteria: they glow green and make the protein (Chalfie 1994)

compendium.periodic_elements.tree.oak.ab: A broad, long-lived tree with lobed leaves and acorns. One oak can host hundreds of insect species, and its timber built Europe's ships and cathedrals for a thousand years.
A slender pioneer with white bark that peels in papery strips. Birch bark is waterproof and burns even when damp; people made canoes, boxes and the first written letters of Novgorod on it.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.spruce: A tall conical conifer with short square needles and hanging cones. Its light, even-grained wood gives the soundboards of violins and pianos; it is the classic Christmas tree.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.jungle: A tree of this world only: a towering rainforest trunk hung with vines and cocoa pods. Real rainforests hold hundreds of tree species in a single hectare instead.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.acacia: The umbrella thorn: a flat crown of tiny leaves on a forked trunk, armed with long spines. Giraffes reach past the thorns with tongues half a metre long.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.dark_o: A tree of this world only: a thick four-trunked oak that shades the forest floor so deeply that mushrooms grow huge beneath it.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.mangro: The red mangrove stands on arching stilt roots in salt water. Its seeds sprout while still on the tree and drop as spears that float for months before rooting.
Tropical Atlantic and eastern Pacific coasts
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.cherry: The Japanese flowering cherry: grown for its clouds of pink blossom, not for fruit. Its brief bloom each spring is celebrated in Japan as hanami.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.azalea: Azaleas are shrubby rhododendrons with funnel-shaped flowers. Honey from some species is poisonous; in this world they mark the lush caves below.
Mountains of Asia, Europe and North America
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.mahoga: Big-leaf mahogany: a straight giant with reddish, stable timber. Centuries of logging for fine furniture made it rare, and its trade is now controlled by treaty.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.brazil: One of the tallest Amazon trees. Its nuts grow inside a hard ball the size of a coconut that only the agouti can gnaw open; the agouti buries the spare nuts and plants new trees.
A thorny tree with orange-red heartwood that gave Brazil its name. Its red dye was shipped to Europe from 1501; today its wood makes the finest violin bows.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.sapodi: An evergreen with sweet brown fruit that tastes of pear and malt. Its milky latex, chicle, was the original chewing gum.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.andiro: A rainforest relative of mahogany with large woody fruits. The bitter oil pressed from its seeds is used against insect bites and as a lamp oil.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.acai.a: A slender palm that grows in clumps on flooded riverbanks. Its purple berries are a staple food at the mouth of the Amazon, and its heart is eaten as palm heart.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.babass: A tall palm with huge upright fronds. Its hard nuts hold an oil much like coconut oil; women in Maranhão crack them by hand with an axe and a club.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.copaib: A tree whose trunk holds an oily resin that flows from a drilled hole. Copaiba balsam was sold in European pharmacies from the 1600s.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.cincho: A small Andean tree whose bitter bark holds quinine, the first cure for malaria. It appears on the coat of arms of Peru.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.oil_pa: A feather palm whose orange fruit bunches give palm oil, the most produced vegetable oil on Earth. One bunch can weigh 40 kilograms.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.teak.a: A tall deciduous tree with leaves as big as a dinner plate. Its oily golden wood resists water and termites, so it was the timber of ship decks.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.cinnam: An evergreen laurel whose inner bark, peeled and dried, curls into cinnamon sticks. Its scent comes from cinnamaldehyde.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.campho: A broad evergreen whose leaves smell of camphor when crushed. Camphor distilled from its wood made celluloid, the first plastic film.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.sal.ab: A tall, nearly evergreen tree that forms whole forests. Its hard wood frames Indian houses and its resin is burned as incense; the Buddha is said to have been born under one.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.sal.ra: Himalayan foothills of India and Nepal
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.nutmeg: An evergreen whose seed is nutmeg and whose red seed lace is mace. Wars were fought over the tiny Banda Islands where it alone grew.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.baobab: A huge bottle-shaped trunk that stores water for the dry season. Baobabs can live more than 2,000 years; their dry fruit pulp is rich in vitamin C.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.gum_ar: A small thorny tree of the Sahel. Its sap hardens into gum arabic, used in soft drinks, stamps, watercolours and printing inks.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.marula: A savanna tree with plum-sized yellow fruits loved by elephants. The fruit is made into beer and liqueur, and its nuts give a stable oil.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.shea.a: A slow-growing tree that first fruits after 15 years. Its nuts give shea butter, a fat used in food, soap and chocolate.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.eucaly: The Tasmanian blue gum: a fast-growing giant with peeling bark and blue juvenile leaves. Its oil, eucalyptol, clears the nose; its plantations feed paper mills worldwide.
A twisted cerrado tree with a yellow, strongly scented fruit. Under the pulp the seed hides fine spines, so the fruit is gnawed, never bitten.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.barbat: A small cerrado tree with thick corky bark. The bark is so rich in tannin that it was used to tan leather and to treat wounds.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.yellow: In the dry season it drops every leaf and flowers bright yellow. Its wood, ipê, is one of the hardest and densest timbers in the world.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.jatoba: A large tree with paired leaflets and pods full of sweet, powdery pulp. Its resin, copal, hardened into amber over millions of years.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.sandal: A half-parasite whose roots tap other plants' roots for water. Its scented heartwood and oil are so valuable that wild trees have been cut almost out.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.dragon: An umbrella of stiff leaves on thick branches, found only on Socotra. Its red resin, dragon's blood, was a pigment and varnish in the ancient world.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.franki: A small tree that grows on bare rock. Cuts in its papery bark weep a milky resin that dries into frankincense, traded across Arabia for 5,000 years.
A spiny shrubby tree of dry stony ground. Its reddish resin, myrrh, was used for perfume, medicine and embalming in ancient Egypt.
Horn of Africa and southern Arabia
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.date_p: The desert's crop palm, grown in oases for at least 7,000 years. Female trees bear clusters of up to a thousand dates each.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.mesqui: A thorny tree with roots that can reach water 50 metres down. Its sweet pods feed cattle and were ground into flour by desert peoples.
Mexico, Central America and the Caribbean
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.joshua: A giant yucca with spiky branching arms, not a true tree. Only one moth pollinates its flowers, and the moth's larvae eat only its seeds.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.saxaul: A leafless desert tree with green twigs instead of leaves. Its wood is so dense it sinks in water and burns like coal.
A thorny, drought-proof tree that goats climb to eat the fruit. Its kernels give argan oil, used in cooking and cosmetics.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.palo_v: Its name means green stick: the bark is green and does most of the photosynthesis once the tiny leaves fall in drought. In spring it turns bright yellow with flowers.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.pinyon: A small, slow pine of dry hills. Its large nuts were a main food of the peoples of the Great Basin and are still picked every autumn.
Colorado Plateau and the US Southwest
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.utah_j: A gnarled juniper of dry slopes that can live 650 years. Its blue berry-like cones are really fleshy cones, eaten by birds.
Great Basin and the Colorado Plateau
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.desert: One of the heaviest woods in the world: it sinks in water. Many desert plants start their lives in its shade, so it is called a nurse tree.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.tamari: A salt cedar with tiny scale leaves that sweat salt. It grows where the ground water is too salty for other trees.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.ponder: A tall pine with orange plated bark that smells of vanilla on warm days. Its thick bark lets it survive the low fires that sweep its forests.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.gambel: A shrubby oak that spreads by roots into thickets. Its acorns fed deer, turkeys and the peoples of the region.
US Southwest and the Rocky Mountains
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.mounta: Not a mahogany but a rose relative. Its seeds carry a feathery tail that twists with humidity and drills the seed into the soil.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.elepha: A squat tree with a swollen, water-storing trunk and papery peeling bark. Its twigs smell of turpentine and give a copal resin.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.coconu: The palm of tropical beaches. Its nut floats and stays alive for months at sea, which is how it spread across the oceans.
Tropical shores of the Indian and Pacific Oceans
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.tropic: A beach tree with tiered branches and big leaves that turn red before falling. Its seeds taste like almonds, and its fallen leaves tint water brown with tannin.
Tropical Asia, Australia and the Pacific
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.casuar: It looks like a pine but is a flowering tree with jointed green twigs. Its roots fix nitrogen, so it grows on bare sand.
Southeast Asia, Australia and the Pacific
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.screw_: Leaves spiral round the trunk like a screw, and prop roots hold it upright in sand. Its leaves are woven into mats and roofs.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.sea_gr: A salt-tolerant beach tree with round leathery leaves. Its purple fruits hang in grape-like bunches and make a tart jelly.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.black_: A mangrove whose roots send up pencil-like breathing shoots through the mud. It pushes out salt through its leaves, which glitter with crystals.
Tropical Atlantic and Pacific coasts of the Americas
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.white_: It grows on the landward side of the mangrove. Two small glands at the base of each leaf give off sugar and salt.
Tropical Atlantic coasts of the Americas and West Africa
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.button: A mangrove of the upper shore with button-like seed heads. Its dense wood was burned for charcoal in the Caribbean.
Tropical coasts of the Americas and West Africa
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.nipa_p: A stemless palm whose trunk runs under the mud, with only the fronds above. Its sweet sap is tapped for sugar, vinegar and alcohol.
Mangroves of Asia and the western Pacific
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.buriti: A tall fan palm of swamps and riverbanks. Its scaly red fruit is very rich in vitamin A; its leaf fibre is woven into hammocks.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.easter: A fast-growing poplar of river bottoms with triangular leaves. In early summer its seeds float away on tufts of white cotton.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.americ: A vase-shaped tree that once lined the streets of American towns. Dutch elm disease, a fungus spread by beetles, killed most of them after 1930.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.ash.ab: A tall tree with feathered leaves and black winter buds. Its tough, springy wood made tool handles, oars and bows; ash dieback, a fungus, now threatens it.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.walnut: The common walnut: a broad tree with fragrant leaves and edible nuts. Its roots release juglone, which keeps many other plants from growing nearby.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.white_: A small tree whose leaves are the only food of the silkworm. Its flower stamens snap open faster than any known plant movement, flinging pollen.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.linden: The small-leaved lime: heart-shaped leaves and fragrant flowers that bees love. Its soft white wood is a favourite of carvers, and its inner bark gave rope.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.sweet_: A broad tree with long toothed leaves and spiny husks holding chestnuts. In many mountain villages chestnuts were the bread of the poor.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.pear.a: The pear tree: white spring blossom and juicy fruit, grown since antiquity. Pear wood is hard and fine enough to cut printing blocks and rulers.
A shrubby tree with flat heads of scented cream flowers and dark purple berries. The berries must be cooked: raw, they upset the stomach.
Europe, North Africa and western Asia
A tall tree with smooth grey bark and a dense shade where little else grows. Its small nuts, beechmast, fattened pigs in autumn.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.sugar_: In late winter its sap rises with about 3% sugar; forty litres boil down to one litre of syrup. Its leaf is on the flag of Canada.
Eastern Canada and the northeast United States
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.hornbe: A tree with fluted grey trunk and the hardest wood in Europe. It made cogs for mills, butchers' blocks and piano hammers.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.southe: An evergreen with glossy leaves and huge white flowers that smell of lemon. Magnolias are an old lineage, pollinated by beetles before bees existed.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.tulip_: One of the tallest hardwoods in the east, with leaves shaped like a tulip's outline and green-and-orange tulip-like flowers.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.paulow: One of the fastest-growing trees, with huge leaves and violet flowers. In Japan its light wood made the chests given to daughters on marriage.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.judas_: In spring pink-purple flowers burst straight out of its trunk and branches before the leaves. The flowers are edible and taste sweet and sour.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.quakin: Its leaves tremble at the slightest breeze. One aspen grove in Utah, Pando, is a single plant with 47,000 stems sharing one root system.
Canada and the western United States
A riverside tree whose roots fix nitrogen with bacteria. Its wood lasts under water: Venice stands on alder piles.
Europe, North Africa and western Asia
A small tree with feathered leaves and bunches of scarlet berries that birds strip in autumn. Sorbic acid, a common food preservative, was first found in them.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.black_: A forest cherry with dark flaky bark. Its reddish-brown wood is prized for furniture; its leaves and seeds are poisonous to cattle.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.yew.ab: A dark evergreen that can live over 2,000 years. Almost every part is poisonous; its springy wood made the English longbow, and its relative gave the cancer drug taxol.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.yew.ra: Europe, North Africa and western Asia
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.black_: A tall walnut with dark, prized timber and thick-shelled nuts. The green husks stain hands and cloth dark brown.
An evergreen with spiny glossy leaves; only female trees bear the red berries. Upper leaves out of reach of browsing deer often lose their spines.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.bald_c: A swamp conifer that drops its needles in winter. Knobby 'knees' rise from its roots above the water; its wood resists rot for centuries.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.water_: A swamp tree with a swollen base standing in water for months. Bees make a pale honey from its flowers that never crystallises.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.white_: A riverside willow with silvery leaves. Its bark holds salicin, the natural model for aspirin; a hybrid of it gives the wood of cricket bats.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.red_ma: The most common tree in eastern North America, red in flower, stalk and autumn leaf. Its sap is tapped too, but gives less sugar than sugar maple.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.ginkgo: A living fossil, the last of a group that grew with the dinosaurs. Its fan leaves turn gold at once in autumn; six ginkgos survived the Hiroshima bomb.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.japane: A small maple with deeply cut leaves that blaze red in autumn. Japanese gardeners have bred hundreds of forms over three centuries.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.sugi.a: Japan's national tree, a towering conifer planted around shrines. Some sugi on Yakushima island are thought to be over 2,000 years old.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.lacque: Its sap, urushi, hardens in damp air into the glossy lacquer of East Asian bowls. The raw sap burns the skin like poison ivy, its relative.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.cork_o: An evergreen oak with thick spongy bark that is stripped every nine years without killing the tree. Portugal produces half the world's cork.
A gnarled evergreen with silver-grey leaves, grown for oil for 6,000 years. Olive trees can live and fruit for more than a thousand years.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.cedar_: A majestic conifer with flat layered branches, on the flag of Lebanon. Its scented, lasting wood built temples and ships of the ancient world.
Mountains of Lebanon, Syria and Turkey
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.black_: A pine with long stiff dark needles that bears drought, wind and poor soil. It is tapped for resin and planted as a windbreak.
An evergreen with long brown pods of sweet pulp. Its seeds are so even in weight that they became the carat, the unit for gems and gold.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.stone_: The umbrella pine of Rome, with a flat spreading crown. Its large seeds are the pine nuts of pesto and Mediterranean sweets.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.aleppo: A drought-proof pine of hot coasts. Greek retsina wine was first flavoured by its resin, used to seal amphorae.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.monter: Wild only in two coastal groves, but planted around the world as a windbreak. Ocean winds sculpt it into flat-topped shapes.
Two groves on the coast of central California
The orchard apple, descended from wild apples of Kazakhstan. Seeds never come true: every named variety is grafted from a single original tree.
Tian Shan mountains of Central Asia
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.balsam: A fragrant fir with blisters of clear resin in its bark. Canada balsam, the resin, was the glue for microscope slides and lenses because it has the same refraction as glass.
Canada and the northeast United States
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.silver: A tall fir with silver-white bark and needles with two white bands beneath. It was the first Christmas tree of Alsace.
Mountains of central and southern Europe
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.dougla: One of the tallest trees on Earth, with cones whose bracts look like mouse tails. Its strong timber built bridges, ships' masts and houses.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.siberi: A narrow fir of the taiga, very hardy to cold. Oil distilled from its needles is used in medicine and scented soap.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.green_: A bushy alder of avalanche paths and tundra. It bends under snow without breaking and fixes nitrogen in poor soils.
Mountains and tundra of the northern hemisphere
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.sycamo: A large maple with winged seeds that spin like helicopters. Its pale wood makes the backs of violins and kitchen tables.
Mountains of central and southern Europe
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.atlas_: A mountain cedar with blue-green needles in tufts. Barbary macaques live in its forests, which shrink from drought and overgrazing.
Atlas Mountains of Morocco and Algeria
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.siberi: The Siberian 'cedar', a five-needled pine with large wingless nuts. Nutcrackers spread its seeds by burying them for winter.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.wester: A huge conifer of rainy coasts with stringy bark. Its rot-proof wood gave the peoples of the coast their canoes, houses and totem poles.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.sea_bu: A thorny shrub of dunes and gravel with silvery leaves. Its orange berries cling to the branches and are rich in vitamin C and oil.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.europe: A conifer that turns gold and drops its needles every autumn. Its resin, Venice turpentine, was used by painters, and its wood resists rot.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.dahuri: The northernmost tree on Earth, growing on permafrost at 72° north. It survives winters below minus 60 °C.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.siberi: A creeping pine that lies flat under the snow in winter and rises again in spring. Its nuts feed bears and sables.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.easter: The tallest tree of eastern North America, with soft needles in fives. The British crown reserved the biggest ones for the masts of its navy.
Eastern Canada and the northeast United States
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.bristl: The oldest living trees: one, Methuselah, is over 4,800 years old. Their rings have been used to calibrate radiocarbon dating.
White Mountains and the Great Basin, USA
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.swiss_: A slow, five-needled pine near the tree line, with fragrant wood used for alpine rooms. Its seeds are spread by the spotted nutcracker.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.whiteb: A high-mountain pine whose cones never open by themselves; Clark's nutcracker breaks them. Blister rust and beetles are killing it.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.lodgep: Straight and slim, used by plains peoples for tipi poles. Many of its cones open only in the heat of a forest fire.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.mounta: A low, many-stemmed pine of the alpine tree line that holds snow and soil on steep slopes. Its oil is used in cough remedies.
Mountains of central and southern Europe
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.scots_: The most widespread pine in the world, with orange upper bark. Its resin gave turpentine and pine tar for the ropes and hulls of sailing ships.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.arctic: A tree only a hand high that creeps over the tundra. Its stems may be centuries old; its leaves feed musk oxen and hares.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.coast_: The tallest trees on Earth: Hyperion stands 116 metres. Fog from the Pacific gives them water in the dry summer.
Coast of northern California and southern Oregon
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.giant_: The largest trees by volume: the General Sherman tree weighs about 2,000 tonnes. Its bark is half a metre thick and shrugs off fire.
Western slopes of the Sierra Nevada
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.wester: A shade-loving conifer with a drooping top that grows up under other trees. Its bark is rich in tannin and its pulp makes paper.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.common: The most widespread conifer on Earth, a shrub of heaths and tundra. Its blue cones, juniper berries, flavour gin.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.arauca: A candelabra-shaped conifer whose branches end in tufts at the top. Its big seeds, pinhão, are an autumn food in southern Brazil; logging left only a few percent of its forests.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.brazil: Jacarandá-da-bahia: dark, scented, streaked heartwood once the finest for guitars and furniture. Since 1992 its international trade is banned.
A large evergreen grown for 4,000 years for its sweet fruit. Its sap and peel hold the same irritant as poison ivy, a relative.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.avocad: An evergreen laurel whose fruit is rich in oil, not sugar. Its big seed may have been spread by giant ground sloths that are now extinct.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.cashew: The nut hangs below a fleshy 'apple' that is eaten as fruit or juice. The shell holds a caustic oil, so the nuts are roasted before they are opened.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.orange: The sweet orange, an ancient cross of pomelo and mandarin. Brazil grows more oranges than any other country.
A thorny evergreen whose sour fruit is rich in vitamin C and citric acid. A ration of lemon juice protected sailors from scurvy.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.papaya: A fast, soft-stemmed tree that fruits in its first year. Its latex holds papain, an enzyme that breaks down meat.
A giant with buttress roots that towers over the rainforest canopy. Its pods give a light, waterproof fibre that once filled life jackets; the Maya held it sacred.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.sweet_: The wild cherry, parent of the sweet orchard cherries. Its reddish wood is prized by cabinet makers, and birds spread its stones.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.plum.a: The European plum, an ancient hybrid grown in orchards. Dried plums are prunes; its blue fruit has a powdery bloom of wax.
A small tree with pink spring blossom and velvety fruit. In China the peach stands for long life.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.aprico: An early-flowering fruit tree of dry mountains. Its kernels give an oil and, raw, a bitter poison like bitter almonds.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.fig.ab: Its 'fruit' is an inside-out flower head, pollinated by a tiny wasp that crawls inside. Figs were among the first plants people ever cultivated.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.pomegr: A shrubby tree whose leathery fruit holds hundreds of juicy red seeds. Its rind is rich in tannin and dyed oriental carpets.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.almond: A relative of the peach grown for its seed. Wild almonds are bitter and poisonous; a single lost gene made the sweet almond people eat.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.pistac: A desert tree whose ripe nuts split their shells open. Male and female trees are separate, so orchards plant one male for every eight females.
A many-stemmed shrubby tree with catkins in late winter. Its straight shoots were woven into fences, and divining rods were cut from it.
A tall hickory of river bottoms with sweet, thin-shelled nuts. It was a food of Native Americans long before it became a crop.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.plane_: A broad shade tree with bark that flakes off in patches. Hippocrates is said to have taught under one on the island of Kos.
compendium.periodic_elements.tree.horse_: A broad tree with candles of white flowers and shiny brown conkers. Its seeds are poisonous to people despite the name.
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.guara: A climbing shrub of the Amazon whose red fruits split open to show black seeds like eyes. The seeds hold up to 4% caffeine, more than coffee beans.
Amazon basin, in Brazil and Venezuela
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.annat: Its spiny red pods hold seeds coated in an orange-red pigment, bixin. Amazon peoples paint their bodies with it, and it still colours cheese and butter.
Tropical America, from Mexico to Brazil
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.ipeca: A small shrub of the rainforest floor whose ringed roots hold emetine. Ipecac syrup made from them was given for centuries to make people vomit up poisons.
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.jabor: Its leaves hold pilocarpine, which makes the pupil of the eye shrink; it is still the eye drop for glaucoma. Wild plants were nearly all picked out.
Northeast Brazil, in Maranhão and Pará
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.malag: A small woody pepper whose tiny red fruits point up for birds, which cannot feel their heat. The burn is capsaicin, made only in the pale ribs inside.
Tropical America; now grown across the tropics
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.tea.a: Every tea, green or black, comes from this one shrub: young leaves are picked, rolled and dried. Its caffeine is the same as coffee's.
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.tea.r: Southwest China and the eastern Himalaya; grown worldwide
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.jasmi: Its white flowers open at night; they are strung into garlands across South Asia and scent jasmine tea. The scent oil is rich in linalool.
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.holly: A spiny-leaved shrub of the mangrove edge that sweats the sea salt it takes up out through its leaves.
Coasts of India, Southeast Asia and northern Australia
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.pemph: A gnarled shrub of coral shores with wood so hard and heavy it sinks; islanders carved tools from it.
Coasts of the Indian and Pacific Oceans
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.naupa: Its white flowers look torn in half. Its corky fruits float for months, so it has reached nearly every tropical beach on its own.
Tropical coasts of the Indian and Pacific Oceans
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.jatro: A hedge shrub whose poisonous seeds are a third oil. Cape Verde shipped them to Lisbon for street lamps; today the oil is made into biodiesel.
Mexico and Central America; planted across the tropics
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.rosel: The fleshy red cups under its flowers are boiled into the sour drink of West Africa and the Caribbean. The sourness is hibiscus and citric acid.
West Africa; grown across the tropics
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.rooib: A needle-leaved bush of the Cederberg mountains whose leaves turn red when bruised and fermented: the caffeine-free red tea of South Africa.
Cederberg, in South Africa's Western Cape
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.calot: A grey desert shrub full of poisonous milky latex. Its puffy fruits are empty but for silky seed floss, once used to stuff pillows.
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.creos: It smells of rain and tar; some clonal rings in the Mojave are over 11,000 years old. Its resinous leaves are up to a tenth NDGA.
Deserts of the southwestern United States and Mexico
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.jojob: Its seeds are half a liquid wax, not an oil. It replaced sperm-whale oil in cosmetics and fine lubricants after whaling was banned.
Sonoran Desert of Arizona, California and Mexico
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.henna: Its dried, ground leaves stain skin and hair red-brown: the dye, lawsone, binds to keratin. Used since ancient Egypt.
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.saltb: Its silvery leaves store the salt of the dry soils it grows in. Herders feed it to sheep and goats in drought.
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.guayu: A small grey bush that stores rubber in its bark. In the Second World War the United States planted it when Japan cut off the rubber of Malaya.
Chihuahuan Desert of Texas and Mexico
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.cande: Leafless waxy stems like candles. Boiled in soured water the wax floats off; it still glazes chewing gum and lipstick.
Chihuahuan Desert of Texas and Mexico
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.sageb: The silvery bush of the Great Basin; after rain the whole desert smells of its camphor. Sage grouse live almost only on its leaves.
Great Basin and western North America
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.sweet: A thorny wild rose whose leaves smell of apples after rain. Its scarlet hips hold more vitamin C than oranges; in wartime Britain children picked them for syrup.
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.black: A dense hedge shrub with long thorns and white flowers before the leaves. Its blue-black sloes are too sour to eat until frost, and flavour sloe gin.
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.corne: A dogwood that flowers yellow in late winter and bears glossy red, sour fruit. Its wood is so dense that it sinks; the Greeks made spear shafts of it.
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.raspb: Its canes live two years: the first they grow, the second they fruit and die. The berry comes off its core hollow, unlike a blackberry.
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.black: The bramble: arching thorny canes that root where their tips touch the ground and take over any clearing. Its berries have fed people since the Stone Age.
Its strong-smelling berries are rich in vitamin C; in the Second World War Britain gave blackcurrant syrup to children free.
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.bilbe: A knee-high shrub of acid woodland floors. Unlike the farmed blueberry, its berries are blue right through and stain mouths and fingers.
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.damas: The rose of perfume: in Bulgaria's Valley of Roses about 3,000 kilograms of petals are distilled for one kilogram of attar, rich in geraniol.
A garden rose from Syria and Persia
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.mock_: In early summer it is covered in white flowers that smell of orange blossom. Its hollow stems were once made into pipe stems.
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.rhodo: Every part is poisonous, even the honey made from its flowers: 'mad honey' felled Xenophon's soldiers in 401 BC. Its purple flowers give a dye.
Iberia, the Caucasus and the Black Sea coast
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.box.a: A slow evergreen clipped into hedges since Roman gardens. Its yellow wood is the hardest in Europe, for chess pieces, rulers and woodcut blocks.
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.box.r: Europe, North Africa and western Asia
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.butch: Its spiny 'leaves' are flattened stems, with a flower in the middle of each. Butchers tied the stiff shoots into brooms to scrub their blocks.
Europe, North Africa and the Middle East
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.wax_m: Its grey berries are coated in wax. American colonists boiled them and skimmed the wax off for bayberry candles, which burn with a clean scent.
Eastern North America and the Caribbean
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.cranb: A creeping shrub of bogs. The berries hold air pockets, so growers flood the fields and the berries float up to be gathered.
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.butto: It grows with its feet in water and bears round white flower heads like pincushions, loved by bees and butterflies.
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.japan: The tea plant's cousin, with glossy leaves and red flowers that fall whole. Japanese women dressed their hair with tsubaki oil pressed from its seeds.
A low spiny shrub with orange-red flowers on bare twigs. Its small hard fruits are too sour raw but fill a room with their scent.
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.hydra: Its flowers are pink in limy soil and blue in acid soil, where aluminium dissolves and colours them. Water it with aluminium sulfate to turn it blue, or with lime to turn it pink.
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.rosem: 'Dew of the sea': a resinous shrub of sea cliffs. Greek students wore it while studying, to help the memory. Its oil is mostly eucalyptol and camphor.
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.laven: Its name comes from the Latin for washing: Romans scented their baths with it. The oil distilled from its flowers is mostly linalool.
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.myrtl: The evergreen of Aphrodite, worn in bridal wreaths. In Sardinia its dark berries are steeped in spirit for mirto liqueur.
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.caper: A sprawling thorny shrub that grows out of old walls and cliffs. Capers are its flower buds, picked before they open and pickled in salt.
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.rockr: Its sticky leaves sweat a fragrant resin, labdanum. Cretan shepherds combed it from their goats' beards; perfumers still use it.
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.sumac: Its leaves are a quarter tannin: the fine Moroccan leathers were tanned with them. Its sour red berries are the spice of the Middle East.
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.heath: The ling of moors, burnt in patches to keep it young for grouse and sheep. It made brooms, thatch and bedding, dyed wool yellow, and brewed ale and tea.
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.gorse: Spines instead of leaves and yellow flowers smelling of coconut nearly all year. Its oily wood burns hot, the old fuel for bread ovens.
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.broom: Green whippy twigs that gave the broom its name. The Plantagenet kings took theirs from it, planta genista; the fibres were spun into coarse cloth.
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.rugos: A bristly rose of sand dunes that shrugs off salt spray and frost. Its big tomato-red hips are the richest in vitamin C of all roses.
Coasts of Japan, Korea, northeast China and the Russian Far East
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.beach: A shrub of the dunes of New England whose small dusky plums are gathered each autumn for jam.
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.bog_b: A grey-leaved cousin of the bilberry from bogs and tundra. Its berries are white inside and were said to give headaches, though the blame lies with the Labrador tea beside it.
Cool and cold regions all round the Northern Hemisphere
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.labra: Its leathery leaves are rusty-woolly underneath. Northern peoples and fur traders brewed them into tea; strong, it makes people drunk, and Scandinavians kept moths away with it.
Northern Europe, Asia and North America
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.crowb: A mat of needle-like leaves on the tundra. Its black berries are watery and seedy, but they keep under the snow all winter and feed birds, bears and the Sámi.
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.cloud: A bramble only a hand high, with one amber berry per stem. In Finland and Norway it is the costliest wild berry, and is on the Finnish two-euro coin.
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.dwarf: A birch that creeps along the ground, out of the wind, with leaves the size of a coin. It is the firewood of the tundra.
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.bearb: A trailing evergreen whose mealy red berries bears love. Its leaves are rich in arbutin and tannin, and were a medicine for the bladder and a tan for Russian leather.
All round the North, on mountains
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.alpen: The rose of the Alps, a rhododendron that colours whole slopes red in July above the tree line. Its leaves are rusty underneath.
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.mount: White flowers with eight petals that turn to follow the sun. Its pollen in lake mud marks the cold spells at the end of the last ice age, the Younger Dryas.
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.dwarf: Perhaps the smallest tree in the world: a willow a few centimetres tall whose trunk runs under the ground. Its bark holds salicin like any willow's.
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.arcti: Four-angled shoots of tiny scale leaves and white bells. Rich in resin, it burns even when wet: the Inuit fuel of the high Arctic.
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.goose: A spiny bush of mountain woods. English growers held gooseberry shows from the 1700s, racing to grow the heaviest berry.
Europe, the Caucasus and North Africa
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.red_e: Its bright red berries make you sick raw, but cooked they made jelly and wine for the peoples of the Pacific coast.
Cool forests and mountains of the Northern Hemisphere
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.dande: Its yellow head closes at night and ripens into a ball of seeds that ride the wind for kilometres. Every part is edible, and its leaves were a spring salad long before lettuce.
Europe and Asia; now on every continent but Antarctica
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.poppy: The red field poppy follows the plough: its seeds wait in the soil for decades and sprout when the ground is turned, which is why it covered the battlefields of Flanders after 1914.
Europe, North Africa and western Asia
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.blue_: One of the very few truly blue orchids. In the wild it clings to tree trunks in cool hill forests; collectors stripped whole valleys of it, and trade in wild plants is now banned.
Hill forests of Assam, Myanmar and northern Thailand
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.alliu: An ornamental onion: a ball of hundreds of small purple flowers on a tall stalk. Crush a leaf and it smells of onion, like its kin garlic and leek.
Mountains of Iran, Afghanistan and Central Asia
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.azure: A tiny four-petalled flower that covers lawns and meadows with pale blue in spring. Small as it is, it belongs to the coffee family.
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.tulip: Brought from the Ottoman Empire to the Netherlands in the 1500s; in 1637 a single bulb could cost more than a house until the market crashed. The striped petals prized then were caused by a virus.
Mountain steppes of Turkey and Central Asia
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.oxeye: The white daisy of meadows and roadsides. Each flower head is really hundreds of tiny flowers: yellow ones in the middle, white ones around the edge.
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.cornf: Once a weed of every wheat field, it almost vanished from Europe when farmers began cleaning their seed and spraying herbicides. Its blue gave its name to a colour.
Southeastern Europe and the Middle East, spread with grain across Europe
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.lily_: Sweet-scented white bells in shady spring woods. Every part is poisonous: it holds heart glycosides like the foxglove, which medicine uses for heart failure.
Cool woodlands across Europe and Asia
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.sunfl: Young heads follow the sun from east to west each day; open flowers face east for good. Its seeds are pressed for one of the world's main cooking oils.
North America; first grown in Mexico about 4,000 years ago
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.lilac: A shrub of the olive family with clusters of fragrant purple flowers in late spring. It grows wild only on Balkan hillsides, but gardens have carried it around the world.
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.rose_: The dog rose climbs through hedges on hooked thorns. Its red hips hold more vitamin C than oranges; in wartime Britain children gathered them to make syrup.
Europe, northwest Africa and western Asia
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.peony: Large pink flowers whose buds weep sugar that ants come to drink. Bred in China for more than a thousand years, it is called the king of flowers there.
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.pitch: A meat-eating plant of poor, wet soils: its leaves are jars of rainwater where insects drown and are digested. In this world it grows only from ancient seeds that sniffers dig up.
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.grass: Meadow grass, the grass of pastures and lawns. Grasses grow from the base of the leaf, not the tip, so they survive grazing and mowing that would kill most plants.
Europe, northern Asia and North America
Bracken is older than any flower: it has no flowers or seeds and spreads by spores and creeping underground stems. Its fronds are poisonous to cattle and horses.
Almost worldwide, on every continent but Antarctica
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.dead_: Not dead, only waiting: the creosote bush stops growing in drought and turns green after rain. A ring of its clones in the Mojave, King Clone, is about 11,700 years old.
Deserts of the southwestern United States and northern Mexico
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.sweet: The lingonberry, a low evergreen shrub of the northern forest. Its tart red berries keep all winter without spoiling, thanks to their own benzoic acid.
Northern forests and tundra of Europe, Asia and North America
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.bambo: A giant grass: a moso bamboo shoot can grow a metre in a day and reaches full height in two months. A whole stand flowers once in many decades, all together, and then dies.
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.cactu: The saguaro stores water in a pleated trunk that swells after rain; a grown one can hold over a tonne. It lives up to 150 years and grows its first arm at about 70.
The Sonoran Desert of Arizona and Mexico
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.sugar: A giant grass whose stems are full of sweet juice; boiled down, it gives most of the world's sugar. The plantations of the Americas were built on it and on the forced labour of enslaved people.
New Guinea, where it was first grown about 8,000 years ago
Haircap moss, one of the tallest mosses. Mosses have no roots, flowers or seeds; they drink through their leaves and need a film of water for their sperm to swim to the eggs.
Damp ground across the temperate world
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.wheat: Bread wheat carries the whole genomes of three wild ancestors. It gives a fifth of the calories people eat, and its gluten lets dough stretch and hold the gas of rising bread.
The Fertile Crescent, from three wild grasses crossed about 9,000 years ago
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.carro: The first carrots grown for food were purple or yellow; orange ones were bred in the Netherlands in the 1600s. The orange is beta-carotene, which the body turns into vitamin A.
Wild across Europe and southwest Asia; first grown for its root in Afghanistan
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.potat: Andean farmers grew thousands of kinds; Europe planted only a few, and when blight struck in 1845 Ireland lost a million people to famine. Green potatoes hold the poison solanine.
The Andes of Peru and Bolivia
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.beetr: Beetroot, chard and sugar beet are one species bred three ways. The sugar beet, bred in Prussia in the 1700s, now gives a fifth of the world's sugar.
Coasts of the Mediterranean and the Atlantic, as the wild sea beet
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.melon: The watermelon is about nine tenths water. Its seeds were left in Egyptian tombs, and desert travellers carried it as a flask.
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.pumpk: A creeping vine whose giant pumpkins have passed 1,200 kilograms, the heaviest fruits of any plant. The peoples of the Americas grew squashes with maize and beans.
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.cocoa: A small tree of the rainforest shade whose pods grow straight from the trunk. The Maya and Aztecs drank its roasted, ground seeds; its name means food of the gods.
Giant kelp is not a plant but a brown alga. Gas-filled bladders hold its fronds up, and it can grow half a metre a day into underwater forests full of fish and sea otters.
Cold coasts of the Pacific and the southern oceans
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.seagr: A flowering plant that went back to the sea and even flowers under water. Its meadows shelter young fish and bury carbon in the mud.
Shallow coasts of the North Atlantic and North Pacific
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.lily_: The white water lily roots in the mud and floats its leaves on long stalks, with air channels carrying oxygen down to the roots. Its leaves breathe through their upper side.
Lakes and ponds of Europe, North Africa and the Middle East
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.torch: An ancient flower that grew before the world began; sniffers dig its seeds out of the sand of warm ocean ruins. It looks like a flame but gives no light.
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.pink_: Carpets of small pink flowers under cherry trees, up to four to a block. No real flower grows like this: it looks like fallen cherry blossom that took root.
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.spore: A flower that hangs from cave ceilings and drips a slow rain of green spores. Flowers make pollen and seeds, not spores; this one needs no sunlight at all.
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.dripl: Wide leaves on tall stalks that tip over a moment after something stands on them, like a trap door. It grows in the clay and water of lush caves.
compendium.periodic_elements.plant.glow_: Vines that hang from cave roofs with berries that shine with their own light. Fireflies and some fungi make light, but no real fruit does.
A lichen that glows on cave walls. Real lichens are partnerships of a fungus and an alga or a bacterium; none of them glows.
Leafy vines with no flowers or fruit that hang from jungle trees and swamp oaks and grow downward. Real climbing plants grow up toward the light.
compendium.periodic_elements.mineral.sto: Plain grey stone, the bulk of the world under the soil. Its composition is the average of the upper continental crust.
It stands for the crust as a whole: mostly granite-like rock that cooled from magma, much of it since changed by heat and pressure.
compendium.periodic_elements.mineral.dee: Dark, hard, layered rock of the depths that splits along flat planes, like slate.
Mud buried deep and squeezed until its clay turned to mica: slate forms where mountains are built.
compendium.periodic_elements.mineral.gra: Speckled pink and grey rock with crystals big enough to see. Kitchen worktops and old city kerbs are granite.
Magma that cooled slowly kilometres underground, so its crystals had time to grow; it reaches the surface only after the rock above wears away.
quartz, potassium feldspar, plagioclase and biotite
compendium.periodic_elements.mineral.dio: White rock flecked with black, like salt and pepper. The Inca and the Egyptians carved it.
Magma poorer in silica than granite, cooled slowly underground, often where an ocean plate sinks under a continent.
plagioclase and hornblende, with little quartz
compendium.periodic_elements.mineral.and: Fine-grained grey rock, the lava of the Andes that gave it its name.
Lava erupted by volcanoes above sinking ocean plates, cooled fast at the surface into small crystals.
plagioclase and pyroxene in a fine glassy groundmass
compendium.periodic_elements.mineral.tuf: Soft grey rock full of tiny fragments. The Romans built with it and made concrete from its ash.
Volcanic ash thrown out in an eruption, fallen and welded into rock.
shards of volcanic glass, pumice and broken crystals
compendium.periodic_elements.mineral.bas: Dark, heavy rock that often cracks into tall six-sided columns, as at the Giant's Causeway. It floors all the oceans.
Runny lava from the mantle, erupted at mid-ocean ridges, hotspots like Hawaii and huge floods like the Deccan Traps.
compendium.periodic_elements.mineral.sha: Dark grey rock that splits into thin sheets. Most of the world's sedimentary rock is shale.
Mud and clay settled in quiet seas and lakes, then buried and pressed into rock; the dark kinds hold the remains of algae that turn into oil.
clay minerals, fine quartz and a little organic matter
compendium.periodic_elements.mineral.gne: Hard rock striped in light and dark bands, often folded like toffee. Some of the oldest rocks on Earth are gneiss.
Granite or sediment cooked and squeezed deep under growing mountains until its minerals sorted into bands.
quartz and feldspar in the light bands, biotite and hornblende in the dark ones
compendium.periodic_elements.mineral.per: Heavy dark green rock made almost entirely of olivine. The Earth's mantle is peridotite.
Rock of the mantle, brought up where plates pull apart or pushed onto the continents in slivers when an ocean closes.
olivine and pyroxene, with grains of chromite
compendium.periodic_elements.mineral.kim: Blue-green rock full of broken fragments that fills narrow pipes; the only rock that brings diamonds up from the deep.
Gas-rich magma from 150 kilometres down that shot to the surface in hours, tearing pieces of the mantle with it.
altered olivine (serpentine), phlogopite mica and calcite, with fragments of mantle rock
compendium.periodic_elements.mineral.lat: Rust-red, porous rock that is soft when dug and hardens in the air; in India it was cut into bricks, which gave it its name.
Tropical rain washes everything soluble out of a rock over millions of years and leaves the iron and aluminium oxides behind.
compendium.periodic_elements.mineral.obs: Black volcanic glass with edges sharper than steel; people made knives and arrowheads of it for thousands of years.
Silica-rich lava cooled so fast that no crystals could form.
volcanic glass, with almost no crystals
compendium.periodic_elements.mineral.cal: White rock of calcium carbonate that fizzes in acid. In the Geological world it stands for the limestone of the basins, where caves form.
Shells and skeletons of sea creatures piled on the sea floor and hardened into limestone.
compendium.periodic_elements.mineral.dri: Stalactites and stalagmites, grown one thin ring at a time; a centimetre can take a hundred years.
Water that dissolved limestone drips in a cave, loses its carbon dioxide and leaves the calcite behind.
compendium.periodic_elements.mineral.san: Tan rock of sand grains you can see and feel. Petra and many cathedrals are carved from it.
Sand of old beaches, rivers and deserts, buried and cemented grain to grain.
quartz grains cemented by calcite or silica
compendium.periodic_elements.mineral.red: Rusty red sandstone, the rock of the canyons and mesas of the American Southwest.
Desert sand whose grains were coated with iron oxide before they were cemented.
compendium.periodic_elements.mineral.ter: Hard bands of clay in red, orange, yellow and brown that stripe the badlands.
Clay and silt laid down in lakes and floodplains, hardened and stained by iron.
clay minerals, quartz and iron oxides
compendium.periodic_elements.mineral.ame: Purple quartz that lines the inside of geodes. Its colour comes from traces of iron and natural radiation.
Hot water seeping through gas bubbles in old lava grew crystals inward, layer by layer.
compendium.periodic_elements.mineral.ice: Ice is a mineral, and glacier ice is a rock. Old, dense ice turns blue because it absorbs red light.
Snow buried under more snow is pressed into firn and then into solid ice, without melting.
ice crystals and trapped air bubbles
compendium.periodic_elements.mineral.san: Pale grains of quartz, the mineral that survives when the rest of a rock has weathered away.
Rock broken by weather, carried by rivers and wind and sorted until only hard quartz is left.
compendium.periodic_elements.mineral.red: Sand stained red by a coat of iron oxide, the colour of hot deserts.
Desert sand that rusted: iron in the grains oxidised in the dry heat.
quartz grains coated with iron oxide
compendium.periodic_elements.mineral.gra: Loose pebbles of every kind of rock, rounded by rolling in rivers and surf.
Rock broken by frost and rivers, not yet cemented into conglomerate.
compendium.periodic_elements.mineral.cla: Smooth, sticky grey earth that holds water and can be shaped and fired into pottery and brick.
Feldspar weathered by water into tiny flakes of clay minerals, settled in still water.
compendium.periodic_elements.mineral.dir: Soil: weathered rock mixed with humus, water, air and countless living things. A handful holds billions of bacteria.
Rock weathered in place and mixed with the remains of plants and animals over thousands of years.
compendium.periodic_elements.mineral.ter: Dark red, deep and fertile soil of weathered basalt. Brazil's coffee frontier followed it across São Paulo and Paraná.
Basalt weathered for a long time in a warm, wet climate: its iron turns to red oxides and its feldspar to clay.
kaolinite, iron oxides (hematite, magnetite) and gibbsite
compendium.periodic_elements.mineral.cha: Pale, crumbly soil full of lime over limestone; vines and beech woods like it.
Thin soil weathered from limestone; the rain dissolves the calcite slowly, so lime stays in it.
calcite, quartz silt and clay, with humus
compendium.periodic_elements.mineral.mud: Waterlogged soil of swamps and riverbanks. Buried and pressed, mud becomes shale.
Fine silt and clay settled where water stands still.
compendium.periodic_elements.mineral.coa: Black seams of coal in grey stone: the remains of swamp forests buried 300 million years ago.
compendium.periodic_elements.mineral.iro: Rusty flecks of iron oxide. Most iron ore was laid down on the sea floor when the first oxygen rusted the oceans' iron.
compendium.periodic_elements.mineral.cop: Brassy copper sulfide with green stains of malachite, the first ore people smelted.
compendium.periodic_elements.mineral.gol: Grains of native gold in quartz veins. Gold does not rust, so it is found as metal.
compendium.periodic_elements.mineral.red: In this mod redstone is cinnabar, the bright red ore of mercury, mined at Almadén for 2,000 years.
compendium.periodic_elements.mineral.lap: Deep blue lapis lazuli, ground for centuries into ultramarine, the costliest paint of the Renaissance.
compendium.periodic_elements.mineral.dia: Carbon crushed 150 km down and shot up in kimberlite pipes; the hardest natural mineral.
compendium.periodic_elements.mineral.eme: Green beryl coloured by chromium, found in mountain veins; Colombia's mines are the most famous.
