compendium.periodic_elements.mineral.cas: Heavy brown-black tin oxide from granite veins; Cornwall's tin drew traders from the Bronze Age on.
compendium.periodic_elements.mineral.gal: Silvery cubes of lead sulfide that break into smaller cubes; it often holds silver.
compendium.periodic_elements.mineral.sph: Resinous brown zinc sulfide, the main ore of zinc; miners called it blende, the deceiver.
compendium.periodic_elements.mineral.sul: Yellow crystals of pure sulfur grown around volcanic vents.
compendium.periodic_elements.mineral.sal: A white crust of nitre in dry rock, once scraped from cellars to make gunpowder.
compendium.periodic_elements.mineral.cob: Silver-white cobalt arsenic sulfide; kobolds, goblins of the mines, were blamed for its poison.
compendium.periodic_elements.mineral.chr: Black, slightly metallic iron chromium oxide in layers and pods at the base of great basalt and peridotite bodies; nearly all chromium comes from it.
compendium.periodic_elements.mineral.pen: Bronze-yellow iron nickel sulfide that sinks to the floor of cooling magma; the main ore of nickel.
compendium.periodic_elements.mineral.sti: Steel-grey needles of antimony sulfide; ancient Egyptians used it as black eye paint.
compendium.periodic_elements.mineral.ars: Silver-white iron arsenic sulfide that smells of garlic when struck.
compendium.periodic_elements.mineral.bar: Heavy spar, so dense a small piece feels like metal; drilling mud uses most of it.
compendium.periodic_elements.mineral.spo: Pale lilac laths in pegmatite, a hard-rock source of the lithium in batteries.
compendium.periodic_elements.mineral.bor: White borax left by dried-up desert lakes, hauled out of Death Valley by twenty-mule teams.
compendium.periodic_elements.mineral.pit: Pitch-black uranium oxide; Marie and Pierre Curie found polonium and radium in it.
compendium.periodic_elements.mineral.bau: Red clay left when tropical rain washes everything but aluminium and iron out of rock.
compendium.periodic_elements.mineral.pyr: Sooty black manganese oxide; cave painters used it as black pigment.
compendium.periodic_elements.mineral.wol: Heavy black tungsten ore in quartz veins; tin smelters said it ate tin like a wolf.
compendium.periodic_elements.mineral.van: Bright red hexagonal crystals of lead vanadate from the dry oxidised zones of lead deposits.
compendium.periodic_elements.mineral.flu: Purple and green cubes that glow under ultraviolet light, the glow named after it.
compendium.periodic_elements.mineral.hea: Black beach sand of heavy minerals, sorted by the waves; the source of titanium and zirconium.
compendium.periodic_elements.mineral.mol: Soft grey flakes like graphite, but heavier and with a blue tint.
compendium.periodic_elements.mineral.col: Heavy black ore of niobium and tantalum, the tantalum in every phone's capacitors.
compendium.periodic_elements.mineral.oil: Dark shale full of kerogen, the waxy remains of algae; heated, it gives oil.
compendium.periodic_elements.mineral.net: The red rock of the Nether, light and crumbly, that burns for ever once lit. This mod reads it as a scoria rich in iron and sulfur.
compendium.periodic_elements.mineral.bla: Dark Nether rock like a sulfur-rich basalt, sometimes veined with gold.
compendium.periodic_elements.mineral.sou: Grey-brown sand that slows whatever walks on it; the mod reads it as sand with bone and organic matter.
compendium.periodic_elements.mineral.glo: Glowing crystal clusters hanging from the Nether's roof; the mod reads them as a zinc sulfide phosphor, like old watch dials.
compendium.periodic_elements.mineral.end: Pale stone of the End's floating islands; its proposed composition is close to Moon rock.
compendium.periodic_elements.group.rocks: The solid rock of the world, from the stone underfoot to obsidian and glacier ice.
compendium.periodic_elements.group.sedim: Loose grains and soils: what weather, water and life make of rock.
Rocks rich enough in one useful mineral to be worth mining.
compendium.periodic_elements.group.other: Rocks of the Nether and the End, unlike anything on Earth.
compendium.periodic_elements.group.igneo: Rocks frozen from molten magma or lava, deep down or at the surface.
compendium.periodic_elements.group.sedim: Rocks laid down in layers by water, wind and living things.
compendium.periodic_elements.group.metam: Rocks changed by heat and pressure without melting.
compendium.periodic_elements.animal.capy: The largest rodent alive, up to 65 kg. It lives in family groups by rivers and swamps, grazes grass and water plants, and dives to escape jaguars.
A giant cousin of the guinea pig: cavies reached South America from Africa about 40 million years ago, rafting across a narrower Atlantic.
compendium.periodic_elements.animal.tapi: A shy forest browser with a short trunk made of nose and upper lip. It swims well, spreads the seeds of the fruits it eats and is hunted for meat.
Tapirs have changed little in 20 million years; their nearest living kin are horses and rhinos.
compendium.periodic_elements.animal.toco: Its orange bill is a third of its length but light, a honeycomb of keratin. Blood flowing through it sheds heat: the bill is a radiator.
Toucans are woodpecker relatives; the big bill helps them reach fruit at the tips of thin branches.
compendium.periodic_elements.animal.slot: It moves a few metres an hour and comes down once a week. Green algae grow in its grooved hair and moths live in its fur.
Its ancestors include ground sloths as large as elephants, gone since the last ice age.
compendium.periodic_elements.animal.gold: The most poisonous animal known: one frog carries batrachotoxin enough to kill ten people. Emberá hunters wipe their blowgun darts on its back.
Its bright gold warns predators. The poison comes from the beetles it eats; in captivity it is harmless.
compendium.periodic_elements.animal.caim: A crocodilian of mangroves and marshes with a broad snout, up to 3.5 m. Its hide was traded by the million until farms and laws let it recover.
Crocodilians are the closest living relatives of birds, with them the last of the archosaurs.
compendium.periodic_elements.animal.ostr: The largest bird: 2.7 m tall, too heavy to fly, faster than a horse at 70 km/h. One egg weighs as much as two dozen hen's eggs.
Ratites are ancient flightless birds whose kin live on every southern continent: emus, rheas, kiwis.
compendium.periodic_elements.animal.zebr: Its stripes are unique to each animal. They seem to keep biting flies from landing more than they hide it from lions. Herds follow the rains across the savanna.
Zebras, asses and horses share one genus, Equus; zebras were never domesticated.
compendium.periodic_elements.animal.deat: A small yellow scorpion of the deserts with a powerful venom. It hunts insects at night and glows blue-green under ultraviolet light.
Scorpions walked onto land 430 million years ago, among the first animals to do so.
compendium.periodic_elements.animal.dese: A grasshopper that, crowded after rains, turns yellow and gregarious: swarms of billions cross continents and eat a field bare in hours.
The two phases, solitary and swarming, are one species switched by touch: Uvarov showed it in 1921.
compendium.periodic_elements.animal.gila: A slow, beaded lizard of the deserts that stores fat in its tail. Its saliva gave exenatide, a medicine for diabetes.
One of the few venomous lizards; venom glands may be older than snakes themselves.
compendium.periodic_elements.animal.red_: The stag grows new antlers every summer and drops them in spring. Ground and dry-distilled, hartshorn gave ammonium carbonate, the smelling salt.
Antlers are bone grown fresh each year, the fastest-growing tissue of any mammal.
compendium.periodic_elements.animal.wild: The ancestor of the farm pig. It roots the forest floor for nuts and tubers and will charge if cornered. Its bristles made brushes for centuries.
Pigs were domesticated from boars at least twice, in Anatolia and in China, about 9,000 years ago.
compendium.periodic_elements.animal.eura: It fells trees with iron-hard orange teeth and dams streams into ponds. Its castoreum, which holds salicylates from willow bark, was medicine and perfume.
Hunted out of most of Europe for fur and castoreum, it has returned since the 1920s.
compendium.periodic_elements.animal.phea: A game bird brought west from Asia by the Romans. The cock wears copper, green and a red face; the hen is brown and lays olive eggs.
Pheasants are cousins of the red junglefowl, the wild ancestor of the chicken.
compendium.periodic_elements.animal.mall: The duck of every pond and river, ancestor of most farm ducks. Its down, the soft feathers under the outer ones, is the warmest natural insulation.
Mallards hybridize with almost every other duck: a species still drawing its borders.
compendium.periodic_elements.animal.amer: A swamp reptile up to 4.5 m. It digs 'gator holes' that keep water in droughts. Hunted almost out, it recovered after protection in 1967.
Alligators look much as they did 30 million years ago: a design that works.
compendium.periodic_elements.animal.hedg: A small spiny insect-eater of gardens and hedges. It eats slugs, beetles and caterpillars, so crops near it suffer fewer pests.
Hedgehogs' spines are hollow hairs; the family is one of the oldest of living mammals.
compendium.periodic_elements.animal.stur: A huge river fish with bony plates instead of scales. Its roe is caviar; its swim bladder gave isinglass, a pure gelatin for clearing wine.
Sturgeons are living fossils, 200 million years old; dams and caviar fishing left this one critically endangered.
compendium.periodic_elements.animal.peru: A diving seabird of the cold Humboldt Current that nests in huge colonies on desert islands. Their droppings built up guano, sold in the 1840s as the world's best fertilizer.
Boobies plunge from 30 m after anchovies; the cold, rich current feeds millions of them.
compendium.periodic_elements.animal.rein: The only deer whose females grow antlers too. It digs through snow for reindeer lichen; the Sámi herd it for milk, meat and hides.
Domesticated in Siberia about 2,000 years ago, the most recent of the herd animals.
compendium.periodic_elements.animal.moos: The largest deer, over 2 m at the shoulder, with palm-shaped antlers. It wades into lakes to eat water plants and browses willow in winter.
Moose crossed to America from Siberia over the land bridge of the ice ages.
compendium.periodic_elements.animal.brow: A great omnivore of forests and mountains: berries, roots, salmon, honey. It sleeps through the winter on the fat it stored in autumn.
The polar bear branched off the brown bear only a few hundred thousand years ago.
A shaggy ox of the Tibetan plateau, at home above 4,000 m. Herders milk it and comb its down; its dried dung is the fuel where no trees grow.
Its blood carries oxygen well in thin air, thanks to genes shared with high-altitude Tibetans.
compendium.periodic_elements.animal.alpa: Bred by Andean peoples for its fine, warm fleece, sheared every year or two. Smaller than the llama, it was never a pack animal.
Domesticated from the wild vicuña about 6,000 years ago in the Andes.
compendium.periodic_elements.animal.alpi: A large ground squirrel of high meadows that whistles alarms and sleeps half the year in a burrow, living on its fat. Marmot fat was a folk remedy.
Marmots are among the largest squirrels; their hibernation slows the heart to a few beats a minute.
compendium.periodic_elements.animal.stoa: A small hunter of rabbits and voles. In snowy winters its coat turns white save the black tail tip: ermine, the fur of royal robes.
The coat colour follows day length, so a warming world leaves white stoats on brown ground.
compendium.periodic_elements.animal.eura: A forest cat with tufted ears and broad furred paws for snow. It stalks roe deer and hares and avoids people.
Lynxes came back to the Alps and other ranges by reintroduction since the 1970s.
compendium.periodic_elements.animal.ring: The smallest Arctic seal. It keeps breathing holes open in sea ice with its claws. Its blubber gave the Inuit lamp oil, light and heat through the polar night.
Seals descend from land carnivores close to bears and weasels that took to the sea 25 million years ago.
compendium.periodic_elements.animal.walr: A huge Arctic seal with tusks up to 1 m, used to haul out onto ice. It eats clams on the sea floor. Its ivory and blubber were hunted for centuries.
The walrus is the last of a family that once had a dozen kinds.
compendium.periodic_elements.animal.sper: The largest toothed animal: 16 m, diving 2,000 m for squid. Its head holds spermaceti, a wax for the finest candles; ambergris from its gut washes ashore.
Whales came from hoofed land animals; the hippo is their closest living relative. Hunting stopped by moratorium in 1986.
compendium.periodic_elements.animal.gree: A slow shark of the dark Arctic that may live 400 years, the longest of any vertebrate. Its flesh is poisonous until fermented into hákarl.
It grows a centimetre a year and is not mature before 150.
compendium.periodic_elements.animal.atla: A silver schooling fish in shoals of millions. Herring fed medieval Europe; its oil and meal fed lamps, fields and farms.
Herring talk in bubbles: they release air from the swim bladder in sound pulses.
compendium.periodic_elements.animal.mure: A spiny Mediterranean sea snail. The Phoenicians crushed thousands for a gram of Tyrian purple, 6,6'-dibromoindigo, the dye of emperors.
Its purple came from a defence secretion: bromine taken from sea water and built into a dye.
compendium.periodic_elements.animal.cutt: A cephalopod that changes colour in a fraction of a second. Its ink gave sepia, the brown of old drawings; its cuttlebone is a gas float.
Cephalopods lost their outer shell; the cuttlebone is what remains of it, inside.
compendium.periodic_elements.animal.hors: Not a crab but a sea relative of spiders. Its copper-based blood is blue; a reagent made from it (LAL) tests every injected drug for bacterial toxins.
Horseshoe crabs have changed little in 450 million years: one of the oldest living lineages.
compendium.periodic_elements.animal.gree: A small, hardy shore crab that has spread around the world in ships' ballast. Its shell is chitin and chalk; chitin becomes chitosan.
Crabs evolved at least five times from other crustaceans: 'carcinization'.
compendium.periodic_elements.animal.crys: A clear Pacific jellyfish that glows green. Shimomura isolated its green fluorescent protein in 1962; GFP now lights up genes in labs everywhere.
Its glow is two proteins: aequorin makes blue light, GFP turns it green (Nobel 2008).
compendium.periodic_elements.animal.coch: A scale insect that lives under white wax on prickly pear cactus. Dried females give carminic acid, the crimson the Aztecs traded and Spain shipped to Europe.
The red is a defence against ants; the cactus is its whole world.
compendium.periodic_elements.animal.lac_: A scale insect that crusts the twigs of Indian trees with resin. Scraped off, sticklac becomes shellac, varnish and the first gramophone records.
Each insect secretes its own resin shelter; colonies of thousands join into one crust.
compendium.periodic_elements.animal.silk: The caterpillar of a moth that only lives with people. It eats mulberry leaves and spins a cocoon of one silk thread up to 900 m long.
Domesticated in China 5,000 years ago from a wild moth; it can no longer fly.
compendium.periodic_elements.animal.eart: It eats soil and fallen leaves and leaves behind rich castings. Darwin's last book (1881) was about how worms make the soil.
Many worm species of northern lands arrived with European settlers.
compendium.periodic_elements.animal.medi: A blood-sucking worm of ponds used by doctors for 2,000 years. Its saliva has hirudin, which stops blood from clotting.
Overcollected for 19th-century medicine, it became rare in the wild.
compendium.periodic_elements.animal.pear: A large tropical oyster whose inner shell is mother-of-pearl. Around a grain inside it lays layers of nacre: a pearl, in about one shell in a thousand in the wild.
Nacre is aragonite and protein in layers, tougher than the mineral alone.
Cattle give milk, meat, leather and labour. Their dung is fuel and fertilizer; their milk sugar (lactose) and protein (casein) became glue and plastic.
Domesticated from the aurochs about 10,000 years ago; the last aurochs died in 1627.
compendium.periodic_elements.animal.shee: Bred for wool, milk and meat. Fleece is keratin coated in lanolin, the grease washed out and kept for ointments.
Domesticated from the mouflon in the Near East about 11,000 years ago.
A farm omnivore that turns scraps into meat and fat. Rendered lard was soap, candles and lubricant.
compendium.periodic_elements.animal.chic: The most numerous bird on Earth, kept for eggs and meat.
Descended from the red junglefowl of Southeast Asia.
compendium.periodic_elements.animal.rabb: A burrowing grazer native to Iberia, spread by people across the world, where it often became a pest.
Rabbits and hares are lagomorphs, not rodents.
compendium.periodic_elements.animal.hors: For 5,000 years the power of farms, roads and armies.
Domesticated on the steppes about 5,500 years ago.
compendium.periodic_elements.animal.donk: A hardy pack animal of dry lands.
Domesticated from the African wild ass.
compendium.periodic_elements.animal.llam: The pack animal of the Andes, also kept for wool.
compendium.periodic_elements.animal.came: The one-humped camel of deserts: its hump stores fat, and it can lose a quarter of its water.
Camels first evolved in North America.
compendium.periodic_elements.animal.goat: Minecraft's mountain goat climbs cliffs like the North American mountain goat, whose hooves grip with soft pads.
The mountain goat is closer to the chamois than to true goats.
compendium.periodic_elements.animal.wolf: A pack hunter of deer and elk.
Every dog descends from wolves tamed more than 15,000 years ago.
An adaptable hunter of mice, rabbits and berries, from the Arctic to cities.
The red fox has the widest range of any wild carnivore.
Kept to guard grain from mice since the first farms.
compendium.periodic_elements.animal.ocel: A spotted forest cat of the Americas, hunted for fur until the 1980s.
A small cousin of the jaguar's family line.
compendium.periodic_elements.animal.pand: A bear that eats bamboo almost only, 12 hours a day.
Its 'thumb' is a wrist bone grown long.
compendium.periodic_elements.animal.pola: The largest land carnivore, hunting seals from the sea ice.
It branched off the brown bear.
compendium.periodic_elements.animal.parr: A big macaw of rainforests that eats seeds and clay from riverbanks.
Parrots are among the most intelligent birds.
Bees make honey from nectar and wax from their own glands: beeswax, the candle of churches.
Honey bees have been kept in hives for at least 9,000 years.
compendium.periodic_elements.animal.frog: A pond frog that eats insects and is eaten by herons.
Frogs have lived on Earth for 200 million years.
compendium.periodic_elements.animal.axol: A salamander that never grows up and can regrow limbs. Wild ones survive only in the canals of Mexico City.
It keeps its larval gills all its life.
compendium.periodic_elements.animal.turt: A sea turtle that returns to the beach where it hatched. Its shell plates were 'tortoiseshell'.
Sea turtles have crossed oceans since the age of dinosaurs.
compendium.periodic_elements.animal.arma: Its shell is bony plates in the skin. It gives birth to four identical young every time.
Armadillos are xenarthrans, like sloths and anteaters.
Bats sleep hanging in caves; their droppings pile up as guano, a source of saltpetre for gunpowder.
Bats are the only mammals that truly fly.
compendium.periodic_elements.animal.dolp: A clever toothed whale that hunts fish with echoes.
Dolphins and whales came from land mammals.
compendium.periodic_elements.animal.squi: A fast cephalopod; its ink is melanin.
Squid keep a thin internal shell, the pen.
The fish that fed Europe for 500 years; its liver oil gave vitamin D.
Overfishing collapsed the Grand Banks cod in 1992.
compendium.periodic_elements.animal.salm: It hatches in rivers, grows at sea and swims back upstream to spawn.
Salmon find their home river by smell.
compendium.periodic_elements.animal.puff: It swells with water to scare predators; its organs hold tetrodotoxin.
The poison is made by bacteria it eats.
compendium.periodic_elements.animal.trop: Reef fish of every colour; clownfish live among anemones.
compendium.periodic_elements.animal.sea_: Not a plant but a colony of tiny animals that glows blue-green in the sea: a pyrosome.
Pyrosomes are tunicates, distant relatives of vertebrates.
compendium.periodic_elements.biome.deep_: The open ocean over a deep floor: few fish, but whales dive there for squid.
Deep cold water, rich in oxygen: herring above, sharks below.
Deep temperate water where whales and cuttlefish roam.
compendium.periodic_elements.biome.froze: Sea covered by ice most of the year: the home of seals and walruses.
compendium.periodic_elements.biome.deep_: Deep polar sea under the ice.
compendium.periodic_elements.biome.froze: A river frozen over in winter; fish live on under the ice.
compendium.periodic_elements.biome.drips: Caves of stalactites and stalagmites, where bats roost.
compendium.periodic_elements.biome.jungl: Like the Amazon lowlands: hot and wet all year, with evergreen trees in several storeys and a dim forest floor.
compendium.periodic_elements.biome.spars: The edge of the rainforest, broken by clearings and rivers, where palms and light-loving trees find room.
compendium.periodic_elements.biome.bambo: Like the monsoon forests of South and Southeast Asia: a wet season, a dry season, and thickets of bamboo under the trees.
compendium.periodic_elements.biome.savan: Grassland with scattered trees, like East Africa: rains in one season, fire and drought in the other.
High savanna like the Brazilian cerrado: twisted trees with thick corky bark on old, poor soils.
compendium.periodic_elements.biome.winds: Dry, windy, rocky savanna like the Horn of Africa and Socotra, home of the incense trees.
compendium.periodic_elements.biome.deser: Hot desert like the Sahara and Arabia: trees live only where roots reach water, as in oases.
compendium.periodic_elements.biome.badla: Eroded red rock country like the Colorado Plateau, with scrub of pinyon and juniper.
compendium.periodic_elements.biome.woode: The higher, cooler mesas of the US Southwest, where pine and oak woodland grows.
compendium.periodic_elements.biome.erode: Bare, gullied hills like the Sonoran Desert edge, where only the toughest trees survive.
compendium.periodic_elements.biome.beach: A tropical shore of sand and salt spray, like the Pacific islands and the Caribbean.
compendium.periodic_elements.biome.mangr: A tidal forest of salt-tolerant trees on muddy tropical coasts, half land and half sea.
compendium.periodic_elements.biome.plain: Open grassland of the temperate zone, like the prairies, with trees along the rivers.
compendium.periodic_elements.biome.sunfl: Warm grassland and farm country with hedgerows, orchards and scattered trees.
compendium.periodic_elements.biome.fores: Temperate broadleaf forest like that of central Europe, green in summer and bare in winter.
compendium.periodic_elements.biome.flowe: A sunny, flowering woodland edge, rich in ornamental and fruit-bearing trees.
compendium.periodic_elements.biome.birch: Cool forest of birch and other light-loving trees, like southern Scandinavia.
compendium.periodic_elements.biome.old_g: An old, tall northern hardwood forest, like those of New England.
compendium.periodic_elements.biome.dark_: A dense old forest where the canopy shuts out most light, like Europe's last primeval woods.
compendium.periodic_elements.biome.swamp: A warm wooded wetland like the bayous of the southern United States.
compendium.periodic_elements.biome.cherr: Mountain woodland of East Asia, humid and mild, like the hills of Japan.
compendium.periodic_elements.biome.winds: Mediterranean hills: hot dry summers, mild wet winters and evergreen trees.
compendium.periodic_elements.biome.stony: A rocky Mediterranean coast of pines and olives, dry in summer.
compendium.periodic_elements.biome.taiga: The boreal forest that circles the north of the world: long winters and conifers.
compendium.periodic_elements.biome.old_g: Old pine forest with deep moss and giant trunks, like the pinewoods of the Rocky Mountains and Scandinavia.
compendium.periodic_elements.biome.winds: Wind-battered mountain forest of conifers on rocky slopes.
compendium.periodic_elements.biome.snowy: The coldest taiga, like eastern Siberia, on frozen ground most of the year.
Tundra: a cold plain beyond the tree line where only dwarf trees survive.
A cold northern shore of gravel and dunes.
compendium.periodic_elements.biome.meado: An alpine meadow just below the tree line, full of flowers in summer.
compendium.periodic_elements.biome.grove: A snowy mountain forest of firs and larches near the tree line.
compendium.periodic_elements.biome.stony: Bare rocky summits; only stunted trees grow in sheltered cracks.
compendium.periodic_elements.biome.winds: Cold, windy hills of loose gravel with low pines and shrubs.
compendium.periodic_elements.biome.old_g: Temperate rainforest like the Pacific Northwest: the tallest conifers on Earth, fed by fog and rain.
compendium.periodic_elements.biome.ice_s: Polar desert of snow and ice where trees creep along the ground.
compendium.periodic_elements.biome.snowy: Steep mountain snowfields with dwarf pines at the edge.
compendium.periodic_elements.biome.froze: Frozen high peaks; the last trees here are centuries old and knee high.
compendium.periodic_elements.biome.jagge: Sharp high ridges above the tree line, with a few ancient pines.
compendium.periodic_elements.biome.lush_: Not a forest but a cave under one: where azalea bushes grow on the surface, a lush cave lies below.
compendium.periodic_elements.biome.river: A river: fresh water running to the sea, with reeds along its banks and water plants in its bed.
compendium.periodic_elements.biome.ocean: Open temperate sea like the North Atlantic: cool water stirred by storms, with kelp and seagrass near the coasts.
compendium.periodic_elements.biome.cold_: Cold sea like the North Pacific: dark water rich in nutrients, where kelp grows into forests.
compendium.periodic_elements.biome.lukew: Mild sea like the Mediterranean: clear, salty water with seagrass meadows on the sandy bottom.
compendium.periodic_elements.biome.warm_: Tropical sea like the Caribbean: warm, clear water over coral reefs and seagrass beds.
